opus-5.5.text:
I think identifying excellent researchers is actually harder than leading them, and the two problems are connected.

The difficulty in identifying them is that the signals people usually look at, like publication counts, famous labs, or polished résumés, are lagging indicators. They tell you what someone has already done in an environment someone else built. What I care about more is harder to see: whether this person has real taste, whether they can tell which problems matter, and whether they'll keep pushing when an experiment fails ten times in a row. Very often the people with the strongest potential are young, a bit raw, maybe without a long track record. So you have to talk with them, look at how they reason about a problem they haven't seen before, and see whether they have their own judgment or are just repeating the consensus.

Leading them is a different challenge. Truly excellent researchers don't want to be "managed" in the traditional sense. If you over-specify what they should do, you kill the thing that made them valuable. So I think the leader's job is mostly three things. First, set a clear and ambitious direction, so people know what game we're playing. Second, give them real ownership and enough resources, especially compute and data, to actually test their ideas. Third, protect them from noise, like unnecessary process, politics, or short-term pressure that pushes everyone toward safe, incremental work.

There's also a tension you have to accept. You want people to explore freely, but at some point a team has to converge and ship something. Knowing when to let a hundred ideas run and when to say, "Okay, now we all push on this one," is the part I find most difficult. You won't always get it right. What helps is building trust, so that when you do make that call, people believe it's based on the work, not on hierarchy.

In the end, I think the best environment is one where good ideas can win no matter who they come from. If you can build that, excellent people find you, and they mostly lead themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the hard part is that excellent researchers almost never look excellent on paper in the way you'd expect. When I was hiring at DeepSeek, and later when I started building my own team, I kept running into the same problem: the signals we're trained to look for, publication count, top-venue papers, big-name labs, are only weakly correlated with the thing that actually matters, which is whether this person can go into a space where nobody knows the answer and come out with something real.

So what do I actually look at? A few things. First, taste. Can this person tell the difference between a problem that's important and a problem that's just fashionable? If you ask them what they'd work on with unlimited compute and no deadline, do they have a crisp answer, or do they recite whatever was hot on arXiv last month? Second, honesty with themselves. Really good researchers are brutal about their own results. They'll tell you the baseline was weak before you ask. People who dress up every experiment eventually waste enormous amounts of the team's time, and in large-model work that waste is measured in GPU-years. Third, and this one is hard to interview for, stamina. Pretraining is unglamorous. You run things for weeks, most of your ideas don't move the loss curve, and you have to keep caring anyway.

On leading them, I think the mistake a lot of managers make is treating strong researchers like they need to be directed. They don't, mostly. What they need is for you to make the problem very clear, protect them from noise, and then get out of the way. My job is to set the direction, decide what we are not going to do, and make sure the infrastructure doesn't become the bottleneck. If I find myself telling a senior researcher how to run their ablation, something has already gone wrong, either in the hire or in my own confidence.

The other thing I'd say is that the best people want to be around other best people, and they can smell it within a week. So the first ten hires decide everything. If you compromise on the fourth person because you're under pressure to grow, the fifth and sixth candidates you really wanted will notice, and they won't come. It's a very unforgiving dynamic, and it's why I'd rather stay small for longer than most people are comfortable with.

astra-6.text:
I think identifying excellent researchers and leading them are two different challenges. When you’re identifying someone, you can look at their papers and past results, but those only tell you part of the story. What I want to understand is how they think when the answer isn’t clear. Can they identify a worthwhile question? When an experiment fails, can they explain what they learned and decide what to try next? Do they have their own judgment, including the confidence to question mine?

Leading those people requires you to leave room for that judgment. If I already know every step and simply ask someone to execute it, I’m not really making use of their research ability. We need agreement on why a problem matters, but there should be space to disagree about the approach.

The difficult balance is between patience and honest feedback. Research needs time, and you can’t judge every idea by whether it produces a result immediately. But you also have to keep asking whether the evidence supports continuing. A good research environment lets people take risks while being very rigorous about what they’ve actually demonstrated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think identifying excellent researchers and leading them are two different challenges. When identifying someone, I care less about whether they can immediately give the right answer and more about how they approach a problem. Do they ask good questions? When an experiment fails, can they explain what they learned and decide what to try next? Those qualities take time to observe, so working together on a real problem can tell you much more than an interview.

Leading them requires another kind of judgment. You need enough understanding to discuss the work seriously, but you also need to give people room to pursue ideas you might not have thought of yourself. The difficult part is knowing when to challenge a direction and when to let an uncertain idea develop. If you demand predictable results at every step, it becomes very hard to do research.
